title: Nightly backup job for the invoice database
context: You asked for a nightly backup of the **invoice database**. It is **PostgreSQL 16**, about **18 GB**, on one **Ubuntu 24.04** server that runs `systemd`. Nothing is backed up today.

context.cap: Current state. The database and its only copy share one disk.
t: Today: no backups. If this disk fails, the invoices are gone.

context.t: What is settled and what is open

r: Safe default at 18 GB, so I did not ask

context: On Windows Server the scheduler choices would differ, so these answers hold only for this Linux setup.
tldr: Linux server, PostgreSQL 16, 18 GB, one disk, no backups yet.
Open decisions: scheduler, copy targets, retention. Some answers add follow-up questions.
The first option of each question is my recommendation.

qs.q: What should start the backup each night?
qs.about: Something must wake the job at a fixed time. Two tools on this server can do it. They differ when the server is off at 02:00.
qs.why: The missed-run behaviour decides whether a rebooted server catches up or silently skips a night.
terms: A systemd setting that runs a missed job as soon as the machine is back on.

pros: Runs a missed job at next boot
opts.d: A `.timer` and a `.service` file. Logs go to `journalctl`.

cons: Errors reach you only by email
opts.d: One line in `crontab`. Familiar and short.

qs.q: Does this server have a working mail relay?
qs.about: cron reports a failed job only by email. Without a relay the message is dropped.
qs.why: You chose cron, so this decides whether failures can reach you at all.

opts.d: I will rely on cron's own failure mail.

opts.t: No, or I am not sure
cons: One more thing to set up
opts.d: I will add another way to report failures.

qs.q: How should a failed backup be reported without mail?
qs.about: A backup that fails quietly is the usual way people find out they have none.

cons: The webhook URL must be kept secret
opts.d: Slack, Teams or similar. One `curl` call on failure.
Check `journalctl` or a log file yourself.

qs.why: You chose cron without a mail relay, so failures need another way to reach you.

qs.q: Where should the copies be stored?
qs.about: A copy on the same disk does not survive a disk failure. You can choose more than one target.
qs.why: Your server has one disk, so a local-only copy would protect against mistakes but not against hardware loss.

i: A disk failure needs a copy **off this disk**.
A lost site needs a copy **off-site**.
vis.cap: What each kind of failure requires.

cons: Downloads can carry an egress fee
opts.d: Upload each dump to an S3-compatible bucket.
Fast restores from the newest dumps.

pros: Safe from deletion by a bug or an attacker
cons: Space cannot be freed for 30 days
opts.d: Objects cannot be changed or deleted for 30 days, even by an attacker with your keys.

qs.q: Which tool should upload to the bucket?
qs.about: The script needs a program to send each file. The two common choices trade breadth for provider-specific features.

opts.d: A third-party tool that speaks to many storage providers with the same commands.

i: Same commands for dozens of providers
You install and update it yourself

opts.d: For example `aws s3`. Made by the storage provider.

i: Supports every provider feature first, such as object lock flags

qs.why: The tool is called from your script every night, so changing it later means re-testing.

qs.q: How long should old backups be kept?
qs.about: Each night adds about 4 GB compressed. Without a limit the disk fills within a month.
qs.why: This sets the oldest state you can return to, for example after a bug that corrupts data slowly.

cons: About **112 GB**, nearly all free space
opts.d: Dense recent history, sparse older history.

cons: A problem noticed after **15 days** cannot be undone
opts.d: Simplest. Nothing older than two weeks.

qs.q: Is your retention period a legal or contract requirement?
qs.about: You wrote your own retention period. Some rules fix both the period and where the data may be stored.
qs.why: A legal requirement can rule out some storage targets chosen above.

pros: Choices can be checked against the rule
opts.d: Tell me the rule in a follow-up message.

opts.t: No, it is my own choice
cons: No outside rule to lean on
opts.d: I will use your period as written.
